paragraphs: A classifier that estimates stress or emotion can become a scientific measurement tool. But when it learns to reproduce a questionnaire or observation protocol, its predictions sit another step away from the underlying phenomenon. This paper examines how that separation affects correlations researchers estimate between the phenomenon and another variable.

The analysis distinguishes the detector’s correlation with the underlying construct, called q, from the true relationship being studied, called r. Averaged over all measurement vectors having correlation q with the construct, the expected sample correlation with the other phenomenon is qr. This describes how imperfect measurement can weaken an estimated association under the paper’s averaging setup.

The authors also derive the probability of estimating a correlation with the wrong sign. For some sample sizes and detector accuracies used in affective computing studies, that probability can reach roughly 20–30%. Training multiple neural networks with different architectures and hyperparameters provides only limited coverage of possible measurement vectors, qualifying its usefulness for reducing correlation variability.
icml-2019-automatic-classifiers-as-scien.tldr: Imperfect automatic detectors can weaken or even reverse estimated scientific correlations, and varying neural network designs offers limited coverage of measurement uncertainty.

paragraphs: Many neural network explanations examine the gradient of a prediction with respect to its input. The gradient describes how the output changes as input features change. This paper argues that such explanations overlook another relevant component: the bias, or offset, in a local linear description of the network.

For a linear model written as g(x) = wx + b, the gradient supplies w but does not supply b. A smooth nonlinear network can be reasonably approximated locally in this form. The authors observe that the bias can contribute meaningfully to correct predictions, so recovering it can add information about the network’s behavior.

Their bias back-propagation algorithm starts at the output and works backward through the layers. It assigns each layer’s bias to its input nodes while combining accumulated bias contributions. Together with ordinary gradient backpropagation, this recovers the full local linear model. Experiments show complementary, interpretable explanations, supporting the value of examining both local sensitivity and the associated offset.
icml-2019-bias-also-matters-bias-attribu.tldr: Bias back-propagation complements gradient explanations by attributing the offset needed to recover a network’s full local linear model.

paragraphs: General-purpose solvers often have settings that strongly affect how quickly they solve problems. Choosing those settings requires running candidate configurations, which can itself be expensive. CapsAndRuns addresses this search when future problem instances come from an unknown distribution, aiming to find a configuration with nearly optimal expected capped runtime.

Capping runtime limits how long an individual run contributes to the objective. The cap is chosen separately for each configuration so that most instances are solved. CapsAndRuns first estimates suitable optimal caps, then uses a Bernstein race to compare configurations under those caps and identify a nearly optimal choice.

The theoretical improvement concerns the amount of time spent searching. Its guarantee scales, in a problem-dependent way, with the optimal expected capped runtime. Earlier guarantees instead depended on optimal expected uncapped runtime, which can be much larger. Experiments show that CapsAndRuns can significantly outperform competing methods. Together, these results connect configuration-search cost more closely to the capped objective the search actually seeks to optimize.
icml-2019-capsandruns-an-improved-method.tldr: CapsAndRuns finds nearly optimal solver configurations with a search-time guarantee tied to capped runtime rather than potentially much larger uncapped runtime.

paragraphs: Compressed sensing reconstructs signals from a small collection of measurements by exploiting their structure. Traditional approaches rely strongly on sparsity and can require expensive reconstruction. Neural generators offer another way to represent signal structure, removing the sparsity requirement in a recent approach, but recovery through those generators can still be slow.

This paper jointly trains a generator and the optimization process used to reconstruct signals. Meta-learning connects the model of possible signals with the procedure that searches for a reconstruction matching the measurements. The authors report significant improvements in both recovery performance and speed, addressing the reconstruction bottleneck alongside the choice of signal representation.

The work also explores learning measurements under different objectives and derives a family of models based on minimizing measurement errors. Within that family, generative adversarial networks appear as a special case. This connection leads to a proposed GAN improvement using gradient information from the discriminator, extending the compressed-sensing perspective beyond the original signal-recovery task.
icml-2019-deep-compressed-sensing-d0da85.tldr: Jointly learning a signal generator and its reconstruction process improves compressed sensing and yields a connection to GAN training.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation tries to make a model work when its test data follow a different distribution from its training data. The paper examines approaches that align representations of the source and target domains. Although this strategy can make the domains look similar, that similarity alone does not establish good target predictions.

A common justification uses a target-error bound with three terms, while the training procedure reduces two of them. The authors show that this reduction can cause arbitrarily large increases in the remaining term. They identify changing label distributions as a situation in which the problem is guaranteed to arise, exposing a weakness in the usual alignment argument.

The proposed alternative relaxes distribution alignment asymmetrically and overcomes some limitations of standard domain-adversarial methods. The authors specify assumptions under which their algorithm has a principled theoretical basis and report benefits on synthetic and real datasets. The contribution combines a diagnosis of why alignment can fail with an alternative whose justification explicitly depends on assumptions about the adaptation problem.
icml-2019-domain-adaptation-with-asymmet.tldr: Asymmetrically relaxed alignment addresses some failures of domain-adversarial adaptation, with theoretical support under explicit assumptions and empirical benefits.

paragraphs: Recommendation data usually contain only a small portion of all possible user ratings. The missing entries often follow a selective pattern rather than disappearing at random. This makes both rating prediction and performance evaluation difficult: observed ratings may give a distorted picture of how a recommender would perform across all user–item pairs.

The paper combines two ways of addressing this distortion. One estimates prediction errors for missing ratings; the other weights observed ratings according to their chances of being observed. Used separately, these approaches can suffer from substantial evaluation bias or variability associated with those observation probabilities. The proposed estimator integrates both sources of information in a doubly robust construction.

The estimator is designed to provide unbiased performance estimation while alleviating the effect of propensity variance. The authors then use it to jointly learn rating predictions and error imputations, connecting the evaluation correction to model training. Their method outperforms the compared state-of-the-art approaches on four real-world datasets, supporting the practical value of learning these components together.
icml-2019-doubly-robust-joint-learning-f.tldr: A doubly robust estimator combines missing-error estimates with observation propensities to improve recommendation learning and performance evaluation.

paragraphs: Audio analysis commonly separates construction of a time-frequency representation from later analysis of its features. This paper puts those stages into one probabilistic model. It jointly formulates time-frequency analysis and nonnegative matrix factorization using a spectral mixture Gaussian process, with priors that allow amplitude variance parameters to change over time.

That formulation connects the representation of changing sound frequencies with the decomposition used to analyze them. To make inference practical, the authors express the nonlinear model in state-space form. This enables infinite-horizon Gaussian process regression with an approximate inference procedure based on expectation propagation.

The inference cost grows linearly with the number of time steps and quadratically with the state dimension. The resulting method can process audio signals containing hundreds of thousands of data points, making the integrated model usable on substantial sequences. Across tasks using empirical data, the proposed inference scheme outperforms more standard techniques based on extended Kalman filtering, demonstrating benefits from the chosen approximation within this joint audio-analysis framework.
icml-2019-end-to-end-probabilistic-infer.tldr: A joint Gaussian process model unifies audio representation and factorization with scalable approximate inference for changing signals.

paragraphs: Fair classification requires a concrete definition of what fairness means. This paper focuses on the expected prediction losses experienced by groups defined through a sensitive feature, such as race or gender. Its central proposal is that those group-level risks should be commensurate, making differences in predictive loss the basis for the fairness objective.

The formulation addresses two restrictions found in some existing proposals. Definitions built around binary sensitive features do not directly cover more general categories or real-valued features. Other formulations introduce nonconvex objectives that complicate optimization. The authors propose a definition that generalizes some earlier ideas, accommodates generic sensitive features, and yields a convex objective.

They connect this approach to mathematical finance, where risk measures summarize exposure to unfavorable outcomes. That connection provides a framework for constructing fairness-aware learning objectives. One special case minimizes conditional value at risk, or CVaR, and remains convex. The contribution therefore links a particular view of group fairness with an optimization framework that can express it tractably.
icml-2019-fairness-risk-measures-a8c3e78.tldr: The paper defines fairness through comparable subgroup risks and derives convex learning objectives, including one based on CVaR.

paragraphs: Rule-based features let a prediction model express nonlinear relationships and interactions through conditions that people can inspect. This paper studies generalized linear models built from such rules for regression and probabilistic classification. Its formulation explicitly balances predictive accuracy against the complexity of the rule set, treating interpretability as part of the learning problem.

The challenge is that the space of possible rules is exponentially large. The authors use column generation to optimize over that space without first constructing a large candidate collection or greedily boosting individual rules. The associated rule-search subproblem can be solved with integer programming or with a heuristic that targets the same objective.

Experiments with linear and logistic regression show better accuracy–complexity trade-offs than existing rule-ensemble algorithms. At one end of that trade-off, the resulting models are competitive with less interpretable benchmarks. These findings suggest that carefully optimizing which rules enter a model can improve the balance between understandable structure and predictive performance.
icml-2019-generalized-linear-rule-models.tldr: Column generation learns rule-based prediction models with improved empirical trade-offs between accuracy and rule-set complexity.

paragraphs: Multiparty learning combines information held by participants who face restrictions on sharing their data. Conventional approaches often train a global model from scratch through a communication protocol. This paper instead starts from the observation that participants may already have useful local models trained on their own datasets.

The proposed Heterogeneous Model Reuse method, or HMR, defines a multiparty multiclass margin to measure the collective behavior of those models. It then optimizes that margin to reuse the models in approximating a global predictor. The formulation accommodates heterogeneous local models and data that are not identically distributed across participants.

HMR exchanges a small number of examples within a predefined budget, so bounded example sharing is part of the method. Its contribution is to organize collaboration around existing models and a shared performance criterion. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data across different multiparty scenarios demonstrate effectiveness, supporting model reuse as a practical route to learning from distributed data.
icml-2019-heterogeneous-model-reuse-via-.tldr: HMR combines heterogeneous existing local models through a multiparty margin objective and a predefined budget for sharing examples.

paragraphs: Imitation learning seeks to learn a good decision-making policy from demonstrations. In practice, collecting optimal demonstrations can be costly, so available examples may include suboptimal behavior. This paper investigates how information about demonstration quality can help a learner make better use of that imperfect training material.

The proposed approach uses confidence scores that describe how good the demonstrations are. The authors develop two methods around this information: two-step importance weighting imitation learning, called 2IWIL, and a generative adversarial imitation-learning method called IC-GAIL. Both incorporate confidence into learning from demonstrations, providing two approaches to the same quality-awareness problem.

A central result is that confidence scores need only be supplied for a small portion of the suboptimal demonstrations to significantly improve performance. The paper supports that claim both theoretically and empirically. Its practical significance is the possibility of benefiting from limited quality information while retaining imperfect demonstrations as a learning resource, reducing the need to rely exclusively on costly optimal examples.
icml-2019-imitation-learning-from-imperf.tldr: Two confidence-based imitation-learning methods improve learning from imperfect demonstrations using quality scores for only a small subset.

paragraphs: Model selection and final evaluation are usually separated so that choosing a model does not make its reported performance overly optimistic. This paper studies a different arrangement: selecting the final model using empirical performance on the test data while explicitly correcting for the statistical consequences of that selection.

The correction treats the performance estimates together through an approximate multivariate distribution. A parametric multiple-testing adjustment then guards against optimism introduced by choosing among candidates. The key idea is to make selection part of the evaluation procedure, rather than interpreting the selected model’s test result as if no comparison had occurred.

Numerical experiments train several common machine learning algorithms on artificial classification tasks. The proposed approach improves the expected performance of the selected model without introducing overoptimism in the reported investigation. The authors also observe a greater chance of a successful evaluation study, meaning it becomes easier to demonstrate sufficiently high predictive performance. These findings concern a corrected evaluation strategy, with its approximate distributional model central to the approach.
icml-2019-improving-model-selection-by-e.tldr: A multiple-testing correction enables test-based model selection that improves expected final performance without overoptimism in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Dropout interacts with ReLU networks in ways that a single fixed dropout rate does not fully capture. ReLUs already deactivate some neurons, so equal nominal dropout rates can produce different effective deactivation across layers. Dropout’s rescaling can also create inconsistencies between training and testing when combined with batch normalization.

Jumpout modifies dropout in three connected ways. It samples the dropout rate from a decreasing distribution, favoring training each local linear piece of the network on nearby regions with high probability. It also adjusts the rate for each layer and training batch so that the effective deactivation rate among active neurons stays the same.

The final modification changes output rescaling to better balance consistency of both neuron means and variances between training and testing. This mitigates the incompatibility with batch normalization. Across several image datasets and different neural networks, the authors report significant performance improvements with negligible extra memory and computation. The result links specific dropout behaviors to a lightweight set of practical adjustments.
icml-2019-jumpout-improved-dropout-for-d.tldr: Jumpout adjusts dropout sampling, effective deactivation, and rescaling to improve ReLU network performance with negligible added cost.

paragraphs: Sparse signals can contain useful patterns beyond simply having few nonzero entries. Standard data-independent linear measurements may fail to exploit those patterns. This paper learns a measurement matrix from data while preserving compatibility with the widely used l1 decoder, connecting adaptive sensing with an established reconstruction method.

The training obstacle is that the convex decoder blocks the gradient propagation needed for ordinary gradient-based learning. The authors address this by unfolding decoding into a fixed sequence of projected subgradient steps. This unrolled computation provides a route to training the linear encoder using reconstruction behavior.

Experiments compare ten algorithms on six sparse datasets, split equally between synthetic and real data. The results indicate additional exploitable structure in the real datasets, with the learned measurements enabling excellent reconstruction using 1.1–3 times fewer measurements than previous state-of-the-art methods. An application to label embeddings for extreme multilabel classification also matches or exceeds SLEEC’s precision scores empirically, showing usefulness beyond signal reconstruction.
icml-2019-learning-a-compressed-sensing-.tldr: Unrolling a sparse decoder enables learning measurement matrices that exploit data structure and reduce the measurements needed for reconstruction.

paragraphs: Kernel exponential families offer flexible probability models that can be fitted through score matching. Their practical usefulness is constrained, however, when a simple kernel must be chosen in advance. This paper replaces that fixed choice with a kernel parameterized by a deep network, allowing the representation to adapt to the data.

The learned kernel can capture local geometric features that vary with location. This gives the density model greater flexibility to represent complex structure in moderate-dimensional problems. The approach builds on the kernel exponential family’s score-matching formulation while expanding the kinds of similarities and local patterns its kernel can express.

The empirical comparison highlights a trade-off between two aspects of density estimation. Deep models trained by maximum likelihood can achieve higher likelihoods, whereas the proposed approach gives better estimates of the score, the gradient of the log density. Because that gradient describes distributional shape, the findings distinguish accurate local shape information from likelihood performance and position the approach as complementary to maximum-likelihood models.
icml-2019-learning-deep-kernels-for-expo.tldr: Learning deep kernels enriches exponential-family density models and empirically improves score estimates, with different trade-offs from maximum-likelihood models.

paragraphs: This paper develops an approximate inference framework for hidden Markov jump processes, whose latent states change through discrete transitions. Its focus is smoothing: estimating the hidden process using observations. The proposed variational approach represents the inference problem through moment functions, providing a structured way to approximate the posterior process.

The central modeling choice is a partition of all possible transitions into classes. From that partition, a corresponding set of moment functions arises. The authors show how to express the Kullback–Leibler divergence from the approximate process to the posterior process using those moments, connecting the chosen transition grouping directly to the variational objective.

The paper considers special classes of jump processes that frequently appear in applications to illustrate possible partitions. It also extends the results to inference about latent parameters and demonstrates the framework on several examples. The contribution is a flexible construction: transition classes determine the moment representation used for approximation, allowing the inference formulation to reflect the structure of the process being modeled.
icml-2019-moment-based-variational-infer.tldr: Grouping transitions into classes yields moment-based variational objectives for approximate smoothing and parameter inference in Markov jump processes.

paragraphs: Text generation usually follows an order fixed before learning, commonly producing words from left to right. This paper asks whether a model can learn useful generation orders itself. Its framework learns those orders without extra annotation, making the choice of where to generate a word part of the policy being trained.

Generation begins with a word at an arbitrary position. The model then recursively generates words to its left and afterward words to its right. These recursive decisions form a binary tree, providing an organized procedure for building a sequence even when its words are not produced in their final reading order.

Training is formulated as imitation learning. A coaching method gradually moves from following an oracle toward reinforcing the policy’s own preferences. Experiments demonstrate that the resulting policies can generate text without a prespecified order while achieving performance competitive with conventional left-to-right generation. The finding establishes the feasibility of learning generation order alongside word choices within this recursive framework.
icml-2019-non-monotonic-sequential-text-.tldr: An imitation-learning framework learns recursive text-generation orders without additional annotation and achieves competitive performance with left-to-right generation.

paragraphs: Optimal transport is useful in machine learning, but computing its transport plan can be expensive. This paper proposes SPOT, a generative-learning framework that approximates the plan through a transformed reference distribution. The transformation provides an implicit representation of the plan and a way to generate samples from it.

The authors formulate the transport problem as a minimax problem and solve it using primal-dual stochastic gradient-type algorithms. This connects transport computation to a learning procedure operating on the generative representation. They also show how neural ordinary differential equations can recover the density of the transport plan, adding density evaluation to the framework’s capabilities.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets illustrate robustness and favorable convergence behavior. Efficient sampling from the approximated plan is another practical benefit, because downstream tasks can use those samples directly. The authors identify domain adaptation as one such application. Overall, SPOT combines a learnable transport representation, stochastic optimization, and sampling within a framework aimed at larger-scale transport problems.
icml-2019-on-scalable-and-efficient-comp.tldr: SPOT approximates optimal transport plans with a generative model, enabling efficient stochastic optimization, sampling, and density recovery.

paragraphs: Sparse linear regression seeks a predictor that depends on relatively few input variables. This paper studies that task under local differential privacy and identifies a sharp distinction between protecting the whole dataset and protecting only response labels. That distinction determines how estimation error can depend on the number of available variables.

When the whole dataset requires protection, the authors prove that polynomial dependence on dimension is unavoidable in both noninteractive and sequentially interactive local models. Related limitations persist for other error measures and relaxed local models. For the low-dimensional sparse setting, they propose LDP-IHT, a sequentially interactive algorithm with a nearly optimal upper bound and applicability to several other sparsity-constrained problems.

The high-dimensional picture improves when privacy is restricted to labels. In that setting, the optimal error rate can depend only logarithmically on dimension, and a label-private version of LDP-IHT supplies an upper bound. Experiments on real and synthetic data support the analysis, showing why the scope of privacy protection is central to achievable accuracy.
icml-2019-on-sparse-linear-regression-in.tldr: Sparse regression faces unavoidable dimensional costs under full local privacy, while label-only privacy permits logarithmic dimension dependence.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning performance on sampled experience can differ from a policy’s expected return. Understanding that gap is difficult because assumptions used in supervised-learning theory often do not apply. This paper studies a special class of reinforcement-learning problems in which trajectory distributions admit a decomposition through the reparameterization trick.

For this class, a trajectory can be computed deterministically once peripheral random variables are specified, and expected return can be estimated efficiently. These properties let the authors connect the reinforcement-learning problem to supervised and transfer learning. They use those connections to derive generalization guarantees based on Rademacher complexity and PAC-Bayes bounds.

The guarantees address the gap between empirical and expected return for both intrinsic and external errors. The bounds suggest that generalization depends on several factors, including the smoothness of environment transitions, rewards, and the policy function class. Simulations empirically verify relationships between those factors and the gap. The resulting account is specifically grounded in reparameterizable problems, where the trajectory decomposition enables the theoretical analysis.
icml-2019-on-the-generalization-gap-in-r.tldr: For reparameterizable reinforcement learning, generalization bounds connect the return gap to properties of transitions, rewards, and policy classes.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovery of a high-dimensional vector represented by a generator with a much smaller input dimension. This representation supplies structure without requiring a dedicated sparse basis. The challenge is to recover the vector when measurements are non-Gaussian, may undergo unknown nonlinear transformations, and produce heavy-tailed responses.

The authors construct estimators using score functions and first- and second-order Stein identities. They prove measurement requirements for achieving a specified recovery error, expressed through exponential concentration inequalities. The general sample bound scales with the generator’s input dimension k, inverse squared target error, and a logarithmic factor, connecting recovery cost to the lower-dimensional representation.

For multilayer ReLU generators, they obtain a sample bound of order k times inverse squared error times log(d), where d is the ambient dimension. This matches the stated statistical rate for recovering k-sparse vectors in compressed sensing. The analysis also develops chaining methods for bounding heavy-tailed processes, contributing theoretical tools alongside the recovery estimators.
icml-2019-on-the-statistical-rate-of-non.tldr: Score-based estimators provide recovery guarantees for generative signal models with nonlinear, non-Gaussian measurements and heavy-tailed responses.

paragraphs: This paper designs neural networks around probabilistic symmetries in data. Its partially exchangeable networks, or PENs, are unchanged by block-switch transformations associated with conditionally Markovian processes. Encoding that invariance in the architecture makes the network respect a specific form of structure in the data it processes.

The authors also establish a representation result: any function invariant to those block switches has a PEN-like representation. DeepSets appears as a special case, so the family includes architectures for fully exchangeable data as well. This connects the proposed network design to both partial and full exchangeability within a common framework.

The application is learning summary statistics for approximate Bayesian computation, where those summaries support posterior inference. Comparisons with earlier deep-learning methods are highly competitive across time-series and static models. The authors report more reliable posterior samples even with less training data. These findings support using the relevant probabilistic symmetry as an architectural guide when learning summaries for the studied inference problems.
icml-2019-partially-exchangeable-network.tldr: PENs encode partial-exchangeability symmetries and learn effective summary statistics for approximate Bayesian computation, even with less training data.

paragraphs: Robustness verification asks whether a neural network’s predictions withstand input perturbations. PROVEN addresses this through probability certificates when perturbations have a distributional characterization. Its guarantees therefore use information about how perturbations are distributed, giving a probabilistic account of robustness tied to that characterization.

The framework builds on existing worst-case verification methods, including Fast-Lin, CROWN, and CNN-Cert. Reusing those foundations allows probability certificates to be computed with little additional overhead. The contribution is a probabilistic extension of established verification machinery, making distribution-aware certification accessible without replacing the underlying verification approach.

Experiments cover small and large networks on MNIST and CIFAR. The authors report certificate improvements of around 1.8 times and 3.5 times relative to the worst-case certificates from CROWN and CNN-Cert, with at least 99.99% confidence. These results illustrate how a distributional view can yield tighter certificates in the tested settings. Their meaning remains probabilistic: the certificate draws its strength from the specified perturbation distribution and its statistical guarantee.
icml-2019-proven-verifying-robustness-of.tldr: PROVEN extends existing robustness verifiers to produce tighter probabilistic certificates under distributionally characterized input perturbations.

paragraphs: Graph convolutional networks combine graph structure with learned transformations to build representations. This paper investigates whether some of their inherited deep-learning complexity is unnecessary. The authors progressively remove nonlinearities and combine the weight matrices between successive layers, producing a substantially simpler linear model.

Their theoretical analysis identifies the resulting computation as a fixed low-pass graph filter followed by a linear classifier. This description separates the graph-based filtering operation from the learned prediction step. It also makes the model easier to interpret, because its behavior can be understood through those two components rather than a sequence of nonlinear layers.

Experiments show that these simplifications preserve accuracy in many downstream applications. The resulting model also handles larger datasets and achieves speedups of up to two orders of magnitude over FastGCN. The evidence supports the usefulness of this simpler architecture across the evaluated settings, showing that graph filtering plus linear classification can retain much of the practical value of more elaborate graph convolutional models.
icml-2019-simplifying-graph-convolutiona.tldr: Removing nonlinearities yields a graph filter plus linear classifier that preserves accuracy in many applications while substantially accelerating computation.

paragraphs: Adversarial robustness depends on which changes an attacker is allowed to make. This paper introduces a threat model based on Wasserstein distance, which measures the cost of moving pixel mass in an image. That perspective can naturally represent transformations such as translations, rotations, scaling, and distortion.

To construct attacks within this distance constraint, the authors develop an approximate projection onto a Wasserstein ball using modified Sinkhorn iterations. The projection supports generating adversarial examples under a movement-based budget. It gives a computational method for testing a form of image variation beyond the norm-bounded perturbations emphasized in much earlier work.

In the reported CIFAR10 experiments, attacks reduce traditional models to 3% accuracy within a Wasserstein radius of 0.1, described as moving 10% of image mass by one pixel. PGD-based adversarial training raises adversarial accuracy to 76%. These findings establish both vulnerability under the proposed threat model and an empirical benefit from training against it, motivating robustness measures that reflect spatial image changes.
icml-2019-wasserstein-adversarial-exampl.tldr: Modified Sinkhorn iterations enable Wasserstein attacks that move pixel mass, revealing vulnerabilities that adversarial training can substantially reduce.
